title: Activity lifecycle
scopeHtml: Scope: callback order and meaning (single and multi-activity), what belongs in each callback, finishing and destruction, Lifecycle states/events, lifecycle-aware components, process-wide lifecycle, and the Activity Result API. Config changes, fragments, process death and launch modes are covered in other chunks.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the Activity lifecycle callbacks in order, from launch to destruction, and tell me what the OS is actually telling you at each step.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline check. Candidates who recite names but cannot say what state each one signals will fail every later question about leaks, multi-window and analytics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "onCreate runs once per instance and is where I build the UI and wire dependencies. onStart means the activity is becoming visible. onResume means it is in the foreground and has user focus. Going away is the mirror: onPause means focus is lost or about to be lost, onStop means it is no longer visible, onDestroy means this instance is being discarded, either because the user finished it or because of a configuration change. There are two nested loops: visible lifetime (onStart to onStop) and foreground lifetime (onResume to onPause). onRestart sits between onStop and onStart when a stopped instance comes back."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The lifecycle is a state machine driven by ActivityThread on the main thread, in response to transactions sent by the system process (ActivityTaskManagerService). Each callback is a state report, not a request.

            onCreate
               |
            onStart <------------- onRestart
               |                      ^
            onResume                  |
               |  (foreground)        |
            onPause                   |
               |                      |
            onStop -------------------+   (user comes back)
               |
            onDestroy
Callback State it means Typical frequency per instance
onCreate Instance exists, no window yet once
onStart Becoming visible 0..n
onResume Visible and has focus (top resumed) 0..n
onPause Losing focus; may still be visible 0..n
onStop Not visible 0..n
onDestroy Instance being torn down 0..1 (not guaranteed)

Key properties: onCreate and onDestroy bound the instance; onStart/onStop bound visibility; onResume/onPause bound interactivity. onPause must be quick because the next activity's onResume waits on it (in the classic single-resumed model). The system may kill the process after onStop (and, on very old versions, after onPause) without calling onDestroy.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DemoActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)   // always call super first for lifecycle/saved state wiring
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_demo)
        Log.d("Demo", "onCreate restored=${savedInstanceState != null}")
    }
    override fun onStart()  { super.onStart();  Log.d("Demo", "onStart") }
    override fun onResume() { super.onResume(); Log.d("Demo", "onResume") }
    override fun onPause()  { Log.d("Demo", "onPause");  super.onPause() }
    override fun onStop()   { Log.d("Demo", "onStop");   super.onStop() }
    override fun onDestroy(){ Log.d("Demo", "onDestroy"); super.onDestroy() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating onCreate as "app start": it runs on every recreation (rotation, process restore).
  • Believing onDestroy always runs (it does not, see the dedicated question).
  • Forgetting onRestart exists; it only fires for stopped-then-returning instances, never on first launch.
  • Heavy work in onPause; it delays the next screen.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which callbacks run when I press Home, then reopen the app? → onPause, onStop on Home; onRestart, onStart, onResume on return. onCreate does not run unless the process/instance was killed.
  2. Is onResume guaranteed to mean the UI is drawn? → No. The first frame is drawn after onResume (see the first-frame question).
  3. Who calls these? → ActivityThread executes lifecycle transactions (ActivityTransactionItem / ClientTransaction) sent by ATMS over Binder, on the main thread.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites the diagram. Senior frames it as three nested scopes (instance, visible, focused), names who drives it (ATMS to ActivityThread), and says which work belongs to which scope.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that put "initialise SDK" in onCreate of every screen discovered it ran on every rotation and again after process restore, doubling network calls.

questions.promptHtml: Activity A starts Activity B. Give me the exact callback order across both, and then the order when the user presses Back from B.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The famous trap: onStop of A comes after B is resumed. Tests whether you understand why saving state "in onStop of the previous screen" is not available before the next screen shows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A.onPause, then B.onCreate, B.onStart, B.onResume, and only then A.onStop, because A must stay alive until B's window is up. On Back: B.onPause, then A.onRestart, A.onStart, A.onResume, then B.onStop and B.onDestroy. If B is translucent or dialog-themed, A is still visible so A.onStop never runs."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The system pauses the current resumed activity first (a hard rule: only one top-resumed activity in the classic model), then creates and resumes the next one. The old one is stopped last because the transition animation needs both windows, and stopping early would show a blank frame.

A -> B:
 A.onPause
 B.onCreate -> B.onStart -> B.onResume
 A.onStop                         (only if B fully covers A)

Back from B (A was stopped):
 B.onPause
 A.onRestart -> A.onStart -> A.onResume
 B.onStop -> B.onDestroy

Consequences:

  • Anything A must do before B reads it (persist, flush) belongs in onPause, and it must be fast, or write synchronously from memory state in a lightweight way.
  • B's onCreate runs before A's onStop, so peak memory includes both activities' view trees. Relevant for bitmap-heavy screens.
  • With Theme.Translucent or a dialog-themed B, A stays STARTED and receives no onStop.
  • With A launched finish() right after startActivity(B), A.onDestroy follows after B resumes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// In A: ordering is observable via Lifecycle events too
lifecycle.addObserver(LifecycleEventObserver { _, e -> Log.d("A", e.name) })
startActivity(Intent(this, BActivity::class.java))
// Logcat: A ON_PAUSE, B ON_CREATE, B ON_START, B ON_RESUME, A ON_STOP

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming A.onStop happens before B.onCreate and so reusing a camera or exclusive resource handed from A to B.
  • Starting a network write in A.onStop expecting B to see it.
  • Forgetting the translucent exception.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't B.onResume wait until A.onStop? → The old window must remain for the transition; the system only stops A once B is resumed and covering it.
  2. A and B both open the camera, which one wins? → B.onResume runs before A.onStop; if A releases the camera in onStop, B's open fails with CAMERA_IN_USE. Release in onPause.
  3. What changes in multi-window? → See the multi-resume question; both can be RESUMED on Android 10+.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gets the sequence. Senior explains the reason, the translucent exception, and the exclusive-resource consequence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A QR scanner screen opened from a camera preview screen failed intermittently with ERROR_CAMERA_IN_USE because the first screen released the camera in onStop, which runs after the second's onResume.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an activity being visible and being in the foreground? Give me concrete cases where onPause is called but onStop is not, and cases where neither is called but the user loses input.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Distinguishes people who map "onPause = went to background" (wrong) from people who know the system's definitions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Visible means any part of the window is on screen, which is the onStart to onStop span. Foreground, or focused, means the user is interacting with it, onResume to onPause. onPause without onStop happens with a translucent activity on top, a system permission dialog, split-screen when you touch the other pane, or Picture-in-Picture. Neither is called for an AlertDialog in your own activity, the notification shade, or the power menu; you only get onWindowFocusChanged(false)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lifecycle callbacks are about the Activity record's state in ATMS, not about window focus. Window focus is a separate WindowManager concept delivered via onWindowFocusChanged.

Situation onPause onStop onWindowFocusChanged(false)
Open another full-screen activity yes yes (later) yes
Translucent/dialog-themed activity on top yes no yes
Runtime permission dialog (system UI) yes no yes
Split-screen, user taps other app yes (API 24-28) / no on Android 10+ multi-resume no yes
Picture-in-Picture entered yes no (until PiP closed) yes
AlertDialog or DialogFragment in your own activity no no yes
Notification shade pulled down no no yes
Power menu / system dialog no no yes
Screen off yes yes yes

Rule: if you need to react to losing input focus (pause a game loop, mute audio), onPause alone is insufficient; also observe onWindowFocusChanged or Window.Callback. If you need to react to disappearing from screen, use onStop.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onWindowFocusChanged(hasFocus: Boolean) {
    super.onWindowFocusChanged(hasFocus)
    if (!hasFocus) gameLoop.pauseInput() else gameLoop.resumeInput()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using onPause to detect "app went to background" for analytics or app lock; it also fires for dialogs and permission prompts.
  • Assuming a Dialog triggers onPause.
  • Releasing heavy resources in onPause and reacquiring on every shade pull (which does not even call it).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you stop a video: onPause or onStop? → Depends on API level and multi-window; see the video player scenario.
  2. Does the permission dialog stop my activity? → No; onPause only, the activity remains visible behind it.
  3. How do you detect the whole app went to the background? → ProcessLifecycleOwner, not per-activity callbacks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "onPause when another activity comes". Senior gives the matrix, and knows that window focus is a different signal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fintech app logged "session paused" on every runtime permission prompt and notification-shade pull, inflating background events by roughly a third.

questions.promptHtml: Where do you put view setup, listeners, sensor and location registration, data loading, and persistence in the Activity lifecycle, and why there?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical judgement: matching the scope of a resource to the scope of the callback pair.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Match acquire and release to the same pair. One-time setup like inflating layout and creating the ViewModel goes in onCreate. Things that only matter while visible, like observing data or registering a broadcast receiver, go in onStart and onStop. Things that need exclusive or focus-dependent behavior, like starting an animation or claiming the camera exclusively in older multi-window-less models, go in onResume and onPause. Persistence goes in onPause/onStop only as a safety net; real saving happens when the user acts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pairing rule: acquire in X, release in the mirror of X. onCreate/onDestroy for instance-scoped; onStart/onStop for visible-scoped; onResume/onPause for focus-scoped.

Work Place Reason
setContentView, view binding, ViewModel access onCreate once per instance
Collecting StateFlow/LiveData onStart..onStop via repeatOnLifecycle no work when invisible
Dynamic broadcast receiver for UI updates onStart/onStop UI only matters when visible
Location/sensor updates for a visible map onStart/onStop (or onResume/onPause if only needed with focus) battery
Camera, microphone exclusive use open when it needs to show; release in onPause or onStop based on multi-window policy exclusive resource
Commit a draft onPause or onStop safety net, not the primary path
Heavy init (DB open, SDK) not in any lifecycle callback; Application/App Startup or a repository lifecycle callbacks run on the main thread repeatedly

Never do blocking I/O in any of these; they run on the main thread, which the system measures (see ANR chunks).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val vm: MapViewModel by viewModels()
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_map)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {   // lifecycle-runtime-ktx 2.4+
                vm.state.collect { render(it) }
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Registering in onResume and unregistering in onStop (mismatched pairs).
  • Doing data fetching in onResume, causing repeat calls after dialogs.
  • Saving critical data only in onDestroy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not do everything in onCreate? → It would keep working while invisible: battery, leaks, stale data.
  2. Why not register a receiver in onCreate? → It outlives visibility; wasted work and potential crashes on stale UI.
  3. Where should a one-time "load data" trigger live? → In the ViewModel init or a first-subscription start, not in a resume callback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists placements. Senior states the pairing rule and replaces manual callbacks with lifecycle-aware observers so the pairing is enforced by construction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A listing screen refreshed in onResume; dialogs and permission prompts triggered extra API calls and made the home feed flicker.

questions.promptHtml: Is onDestroy guaranteed to be called? What does isFinishing tell you, and what are the correct uses of both?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Stops people putting critical cleanup or persistence in onDestroy, and checks whether they know the two reasons for destruction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "No. If the process is killed, for example by the low memory killer or the user swiping the app away, onDestroy never runs. When it does run, it is either because the instance is finishing, where isFinishing is true, or because of a configuration change where isChangingConfigurations is true and the system will create a replacement. So I use onDestroy only for releasing instance-scoped, in-memory resources, never for saving data."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Activity record is destroyed by an ATMS transaction. Process death skips all callbacks because no code runs. Practical corollaries:

  • Persist at user-meaningful moments, or at latest in onStop (the last callback guaranteed on API 28+ before the process can be killed without notice: onSaveInstanceState also runs after onStop on API 28+).
  • Cleanup that must happen for correctness belongs in an observer tied to onStop/onDestroy, but design it so that being skipped is harmless (e.g., a lock lease with a timeout).
  • isFinishing is true after finish(), back press that finishes, or when the system finishes it. isChangingConfigurations is true when a recreate is coming. Use them to decide whether to release shared state or keep it for the replacement instance.
  • Edge cases: finish() inside onCreate runs onDestroy directly with no onStart/onResume. Since Android 12 (API 31), pressing Back on the root launcher activity moves the task to the background instead of finishing it, so onDestroy does not run there; the instance stays in memory until the system reclaims it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onDestroy() {
    if (isFinishing) {
        analytics.endScreenSession()        // really leaving
    } else if (isChangingConfigurations) {
        // a new instance is coming; keep shared state alive
    }
    super.onDestroy()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving user input in onDestroy.
  • Releasing a retained, shared object because onDestroy ran during rotation.
  • Assuming Back always triggers onDestroy on Android 12+.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does onDestroy not run? → Process killed, crash, kill -9, force stop.
  2. Which callback is the last guaranteed? → Practically onStop (with onSaveInstanceState after it on API 28+); even those do not run if the process is killed while still foreground, e.g. crash.
  3. How do I do cleanup when the whole task is dismissed? → You cannot rely on callbacks; use leases/timeouts or server-side session expiry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "onDestroy is for cleanup". Senior says "cleanup for memory only; durable work must not depend on it", and uses isFinishing/isChangingConfigurations correctly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A drafts feature saved in onDestroy lost about 2% of drafts on low-end devices where the process was killed in the background.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to your activity's lifecycle when the screen turns off or the device locks, and what do you do if you need to show over the lock screen or keep the screen on?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps (video, navigation, alarms, calls) hit this, and many candidates have never traced it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Screen off drives onPause then onStop for the foreground activity; unlocking brings back onRestart, onStart, onResume. If I need to show over the keyguard, I call setShowWhenLocked(true) and setTurnScreenOn(true) on API 27+, or the older window flags. To keep the screen on while visible, I set keepScreenOn on the view or FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON on the window, which needs no permission."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When the display goes non-interactive, the activity is no longer visible, so ATMS stops it. After unlock, it restarts. Notes:

  • Sensors/camera/location listeners registered for onStart/onStop pairs get released automatically; those paired with onResume/onPause also, since pause precedes stop.
  • With showWhenLocked, an activity on the keyguard can stay resumed while locked; behavior with the secure keyguard differs per OEM, so test.
  • Activities started via full-screen intent notifications (call/alarm UIs) use setShowWhenLocked and setTurnScreenOn; on Android 14 (API 34), USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT is restricted to calling/alarm apps by default (verify on developer.android.com).
  • FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON is released automatically when the window goes away; no wake lock management needed.
  • Always-on display or lock screen does not mean the process is idle; background execution limits are separate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 27) {
        setShowWhenLocked(true)
        setTurnScreenOn(true)
    }
    window.addFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a PowerManager wake lock to keep the screen on for UI (leaks battery; flag is correct).
  • Not releasing media in onStop and draining battery while locked.
  • Assuming unlock recreates the activity (it restarts, it does not recreate).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the process die when the screen turns off? → No; priority drops, Doze may start later.
  2. How to continue playback with screen off? → Foreground service with media session, not an activity.
  3. Why does my timer reset after unlock? → onRestart/onStart ran; state tied to onStart was reset.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows pause/stop. Senior knows the show-over-keyguard APIs, the keep-screen-on flag versus wake locks, and that background media belongs to a service.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A navigation app used a wake lock for screen-on and drained 12% battery per hour in the background when the release path was skipped.

questions.promptHtml: Why was onActivityResult replaced by the Activity Result API, and how does registerForActivityResult actually work, including across process death?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the design problem (request-code coupling, lost callbacks) rather than just the syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "onActivityResult relied on global integer request codes and a giant switch, and it breaks composition for libraries. registerForActivityResult takes a typed contract and a callback, returns a launcher, and the registry keys each registration, so results are routed to the right callback even after the activity is recreated or the process dies. The one rule: you must register before the owner reaches STARTED, so register in onCreate or as a property initializer, never inside a click handler."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ComponentActivity holds an ActivityResultRegistry. registerForActivityResult(contract, callback) generates a key from a counter (activities) and ties registration to the Lifecycle: the callback is attached on ON_START and detached on ON_DESTROY. Launching goes through launcher.launch(input), the contract builds the Intent, and the registry maps an internal request code to the key. The registry persists keys and codes in saved instance state, so after process death and recreation, re-registering with the same order yields the same key and pending results are delivered when the owner becomes STARTED.

register (onCreate)  ->  key K, callback bound to lifecycle
launch(input)        ->  startActivityForResult(intent, internalCode)
...process may die...
recreate + register  ->  same key K (same registration order)
result arrives       ->  delivered when STARTED

Because keys come from registration order, conditional registration (inside if) can cause key drift across recreation and misrouted results. Contracts are testable: ActivityResultRegistry can be injected in tests.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PickActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val pick = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.GetContent()) { uri ->
        uri?.let { vm.onImageChosen(it) }
    }
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        findViewById<View>(R.id.btn).setOnClickListener { pick.launch("image/*") }
    }
}
// Broken: registering inside the listener -> IllegalStateException when RESUMED

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling registerForActivityResult after onStart; throws IllegalStateException: LifecycleOwner ... is attempting to register while current state is RESUMED.
  • Registering conditionally or in a loop.
  • Holding view references in the callback that is retained.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the callback delivered if the activity is stopped? → Deferred until STARTED.
  2. How do you unit test it? → Provide a test ActivityResultRegistry via the activity constructor/ActivityResultRegistryOwner, or use ActivityScenario with intents stubbed.
  3. How to write a custom contract? → Extend ActivityResultContract<I, O> with createIntent and parseResult.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE shows syntax. Senior explains registry keying, lifecycle binding, and the process-death delivery guarantees.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A permission flow broken in production after a refactor moved registration into a lazy block executed after onResume.

questions.promptHtml: When is onNewIntent called, what is the exact callback order, and what are the classic bugs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deep links, notifications and share targets all route here; bugs show as "app opens the old content".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When an already existing instance is reused for a new start, due to singleTop at the top of the stack, singleTask, singleInstance, or flags like CLEAR_TOP or SINGLE_TOP. If the activity was resumed the order is onPause, onNewIntent, onResume. If it was stopped, onNewIntent comes first, then onRestart, onStart, onResume. The bug is forgetting setIntent: getIntent still returns the first intent."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The system delivers the new Intent to the existing instance instead of creating another. Launch modes are covered in the tasks chunk; here the contract is handling.

  • getIntent() is unchanged until you call setIntent(intent).
  • onNewIntent may arrive while the activity is stopped, so do not touch views assuming focus; set state and let onStart/onResume apply it.
  • After process death, there is no onNewIntent; the activity is recreated with the original launch Intent, so a handler that only processes intents in onNewIntent loses the data on restore.
  • Handle both: one function handleIntent(intent) called from onCreate (guarded by savedInstanceState == null or by an "intent consumed" flag) and from onNewIntent.
  • Consume one-shot intents: clear the extras after use or the same deep link re-runs after recreation (the saved Intent is reused).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    if (savedInstanceState == null) handleIntent(intent)
}
override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent)          // otherwise getIntent() is stale
    handleIntent(intent)
}
private fun handleIntent(i: Intent) { i.data?.let(vm::open); i.data = null }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not calling setIntent.
  • Handling only in onNewIntent, missing cold start.
  • Re-processing the same intent after rotation because getIntent persists.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a standard-mode activity ever get onNewIntent? → No, a new instance is created, unless a flag like SINGLE_TOP/CLEAR_TOP reuses it.
  2. Is onNewIntent called before or after onRestart? → Before, when stopped.
  3. How to avoid reprocessing on rotation? → Guard on savedInstanceState or ViewModel-held consumed flag.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the method. Senior covers ordering in both states, setIntent, one-shot consumption, and recreation interplay.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Notification taps opened the previously viewed order because setIntent was missing and the screen read getIntent in onResume.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Lifecycle.State versus Lifecycle.Event, how they map to activity callbacks, and what isAtLeast means for lifecycle-aware code.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A common confusion that leads to wrong "STARTED vs RESUMED" decisions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Events are transitions: ON_CREATE, ON_START, ON_RESUME, ON_PAUSE, ON_STOP, ON_DESTROY. States are stable positions: INITIALIZED, CREATED, STARTED, RESUMED, DESTROYED. ON_START and ON_PAUSE both land in STARTED; ON_CREATE and ON_STOP both land in CREATED. So 'STARTED' means visible, 'RESUMED' means focused. isAtLeast(STARTED) means visible or better."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of states as nodes and events as edges.

INITIALIZED --ON_CREATE--> CREATED --ON_START--> STARTED --ON_RESUME--> RESUMED
DESTROYED  <--ON_DESTROY-- CREATED <--ON_STOP--  STARTED <--ON_PAUSE--  RESUMED

Lifecycle.currentState, State.isAtLeast(...), Lifecycle.currentStateFlow (2.6+) are the query APIs. Lifecycle-aware components care about states: LiveData is active in STARTED or above; repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) runs the block while the state is at least STARTED. Observers added at any time receive replayed events to catch up to the current state.

Timing relative to the owner's own callbacks (per the DefaultLifecycleObserver docs): create/start/resume observer callbacks run after the owner's corresponding method returns; pause/stop/destroy observer callbacks run before the owner's method. This gives mirror-image ordering, so an observer's setup always happens after the owner's setup and teardown always before the owner tears down.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
lifecycle.addObserver(object : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
    override fun onStart(owner: LifecycleOwner)  { /* state STARTED reached */ }
    override fun onStop(owner: LifecycleOwner)   { /* about to leave to CREATED */ }
})
val visible = lifecycle.currentState.isAtLeast(Lifecycle.State.STARTED)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking STARTED means "stopped is next"; ON_PAUSE also leaves you in STARTED.
  • Comparing State with ==, instead of isAtLeast.
  • Assuming an observer sees every historical event; it sees a replay to the current state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is there no ON_RESTART? → Restart is the sequence CREATED to STARTED; no separate state.
  2. What is the Lifecycle state after onStop? → CREATED.
  3. Can an observer add itself in RESUMED and miss onCreate? → No; it gets ON_CREATE, ON_START, ON_RESUME replayed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists them. Senior gives the mapping, the observer ordering guarantee and replay rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bug where a feature was only enabled if (state == RESUMED) missed STARTED-but-paused situations like permission dialogs.

questions.promptHtml: How should you collect a Flow or observe LiveData from an Activity so it does not do work in the background? Why were launchWhenStarted and friends deprecated?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Very common modern bug; tests knowledge of coroutine suspension semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) inside lifecycleScope.launch, or flowWithLifecycle, or collectAsStateWithLifecycle in Compose. launchWhenStarted only suspends the coroutine when the lifecycle falls below STARTED; the upstream producer, say a location flow or a callbackFlow, keeps running. repeatOnLifecycle cancels the block and restarts it, so upstream collection really stops. launchWhenX was deprecated in lifecycle-runtime 2.6 for that reason."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted {} dispatches using a pausing dispatcher: when state drops, the coroutine is paused, not cancelled, so its upstream flow continues buffering or hot-producing, wasting resources and potentially holding sensors or sockets. repeatOnLifecycle launches a new child coroutine on each entry into the state and cancels it on exit. That cancellation propagates to cold flows and callbackFlow awaitClose, unregistering callbacks.

For a one-shot UI events flow, restarts mean replays; use state-based designs or Channel with care. Hot SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) upstream stops 5 seconds after the last collector leaves, which survives rotation without restarting upstream.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {     // lifecycle-runtime-ktx 2.4+
        launch { vm.uiState.collect(::render) }
        launch { vm.messages.collect(::showSnack) }
    }
}
// Anti-pattern:
// lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted { vm.uiState.collect(::render) } // upstream keeps running

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Collecting in onCreate without repeatOnLifecycle, collection continues in background.
  • Collecting two flows sequentially in one block; the second never runs. Launch each separately.
  • Using STARTED for something that should only run with focus.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How about Fragments? → Use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope with repeatOnLifecycle.
  2. Why WhileSubscribed(5000)? → Keeps upstream alive across rotation (config change gap under 5 s) but stops it when really backgrounded.
  3. Compose equivalent? → collectAsStateWithLifecycle (lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.6+).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE uses lifecycleScope.launch. Senior explains pause versus cancel and picks the sharing policy upstream.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A location flow kept the GPS on after the app was backgrounded for hours because collection used launchWhenStarted.

questions.contextHtml: A video-call feature (800k DAU, 40% Android 11-12 mid-range) opens the camera in onCreate and releases it in onDestroy. After release, support tickets say: "Scanning a QR code from another app says camera in use", and battery stats show the app at 9% drain for users who left the call screen but stayed in the app. Logcat on the other app: CameraAccessException: CAMERA_IN_USE (4)... and in your own app CameraDevice.StateCallback.onError(ERROR_CAMERA_IN_USE=1) shows up when returning from a share sheet. Crashlytics shows nothing. The release is two days old.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move it to onResume/onPause" without understanding multi-window, camera priority, or why onDestroy was late; also blaming the other app's SDK.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the camera light stay on after leaving the call screen? (confirms leak scope). Which Android versions and are tickets from foldables or tablets (multi-window)? Is this CameraX or Camera2? Are we already pausing the preview on screen-off? Did any navigation change keep the old activity in the back stack?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that closes the camera device in onStop (and stops preview in onPause). Add a remote kill-switch for the new feature.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) release tied to onDestroy, but a stopped activity in the back stack is not destroyed, so the camera stays open while hidden; (b) release in onPause breaking split-screen; (c) leaked CameraDevice from multiple opens; (d) other app's SDK bug (red herring since our own app also gets IN_USE).
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys media.camera to see which package holds the device; navigate away and re-run; adb shell dumpsys activity activities to see the stopped instance remains; Logcat tags for CameraService.
  5. Root cause: Acquire/release not mirrored. onCreate/onDestroy pair is instance lifetime, but the resource is visibility-lifetime. A stopped activity in the back stack can live indefinitely.
  6. Fix: Short-term: open in onStart, close in onStop. Long-term: use CameraX bindToLifecycle(lifecycleOwner, ...) so the lifecycle owns acquire/release, or wrap Camera2 in a DefaultLifecycleObserver. Handle onDisconnected/onError for priority steals.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule/review checklist: every acquire has its mirrored release. Instrumented test that backgrounds the activity and asserts via dumpsys media.camera that the app does not hold it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a wake lock, not release only in onPause (breaks multi-window where we should keep the camera while visible), not a global singleton camera manager held by Application.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Android 12+ privacy indicator still shows green dot → means a handle is open; check for a second owner like a background service.
  • Camera should keep running in PiP → keep it open while STARTED; release in onStop, which runs when PiP is dismissed.
  • Two activities need camera in sequence → release in onPause of the first, because the second's onResume precedes the first's onStop.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scanner screen released in onDestroy; reviewing back stacks showed stopped instances up to 30 minutes old holding the camera. Moving ownership to CameraX lifecycle binding removed the whole class of tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames other app or says "just add try/catch".
  • Hire: Identifies mismatched pair and fixes with onStart/onStop.
  • Strong hire: Also covers multi-window priority, CameraX lifecycle binding, dumpsys verification and tests.

questions.promptHtml: What is Application.ActivityLifecycleCallbacks, what is it good for, and what are the limits when used to detect foreground or background?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of app-wide hooks and of why counting activities is fragile.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It is a callback interface registered on Application that notifies you for every activity in the process: created, started, resumed, paused, stopped, saveInstanceState, destroyed. I use it for cross-cutting concerns like screen analytics, crash breadcrumbs, or leak detection. It is not a reliable foreground detector by itself because a rotation produces stop then start, and activity counting needs a debounce, which ProcessLifecycleOwner already implements."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks lets cross-cutting code observe all activities without a base class. API 29 added onActivityPreCreated, onActivityPostCreated, and similar pre/post variants for every stage (also exposed in androidx via ComponentActivity dispatch). Callbacks run on the main thread, synchronously with the activity lifecycle, so keep them cheap.

Counting started activities: started++ on onActivityStarted and started-- on onActivityStopped; zero means background. Configuration changes: the old instance stops and the new starts, momentarily hitting zero, a false "backgrounded" signal unless debounced. Also, multiple-process apps count per process, and activities in other tasks count too.

Do not hold strong references to activities (weak refs or none). Unregister if registered dynamically.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks(object : ActivityLifecycleCallbacks {
            override fun onActivityStarted(a: Activity) { Breadcrumbs.add("start ${a.javaClass.simpleName}") }
            override fun onActivityStopped(a: Activity) { Breadcrumbs.add("stop ${a.javaClass.simpleName}") }
            override fun onActivityCreated(a: Activity, s: Bundle?) {}
            override fun onActivityResumed(a: Activity) {}
            override fun onActivityPaused(a: Activity) {}
            override fun onActivitySaveInstanceState(a: Activity, o: Bundle) {}
            override fun onActivityDestroyed(a: Activity) {}
        })
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaking activities in a static list.
  • Doing disk I/O in a callback.
  • Naive started-count as foreground state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not a BaseActivity? → Third-party and library activities do not extend it.
  2. Are callbacks invoked for activities started before registration? → No; register in Application.onCreate.
  3. What's the difference from FragmentLifecycleCallbacks? → Per FragmentManager, registered on it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "listen to all activities". Senior spots the config-change debounce issue and defers to ProcessLifecycleOwner.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled foreground counter reported 1.4x sessions because of rotation-induced zero crossings.

questions.promptHtml: How does ProcessLifecycleOwner work, what delay does it add, and when would you not trust it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard answer to "is my app in the foreground", and the details expose whether you know its guarantees and limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It is a LifecycleOwner for the whole process from androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-process. It emits ON_CREATE once and never ON_DESTROY. ON_START and ON_RESUME fire when the first activity starts or resumes. ON_PAUSE and ON_STOP are delayed by about 700 ms after the last activity pauses or stops, so a rotation, where one activity stops and a new one starts, does not look like a background transition. It is per process, not per app, and not accurate to the millisecond, so I don't use it for security timeouts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internally it registers activity lifecycle callbacks and keeps counters of started and resumed activities. When resumed drops to zero it posts a delayed runnable (TIMEOUT_MS = 700) on a main-thread handler; if a new activity resumes in that window, the runnable is cancelled. The same for stopped. It is initialized by ProcessLifecycleInitializer through App Startup (androidx.startup) in a ContentProvider, so it exists before Application.onCreate runs.

Limitations:

  • It reflects activity state only; a foreground service does not count as foreground here.
  • Each process has its own instance. An app with an android:process=":remote" component has separate state there.
  • The 700 ms delay means "background" is reported late, and if the process is killed in that window, you never get ON_STOP.
  • Apps with a single activity and transparent trampolines can flicker.
  • ON_CREATE is dispatched when the first activity is created, not at process start.

For session logic, record SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() at ON_STOP and compare at ON_START rather than relying on the delay.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(object : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
            override fun onStart(owner: LifecycleOwner) { session.onForeground() }
            override fun onStop(owner: LifecycleOwner)  { session.onBackground(SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()) }
        })
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting synchronous background callback.
  • Using it for multi-process apps without per-process logic.
  • Adding the dependency but expecting ON_DESTROY.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 700 ms? → A heuristic larger than the typical stop/start gap during recreation.
  2. How would you detect "app locked after 30 s in background"? → Store elapsedRealtime at ON_STOP, check at ON_START; do not run a 30 s timer that the system may kill.
  3. Does a foreground service keep ProcessLifecycleOwner started? → No; it tracks activities only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use ProcessLifecycleOwner for foreground detection". Senior states the debounce, per-process scope, and designs session timing on timestamps.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app locked users out on rotation until the team switched from a homemade counter to ProcessLifecycleOwner plus timestamps.

questions.contextHtml: Product notices that "screen_view" counts on the Checkout screen are 1.9x higher than server-side order-start events (DAU 2M, checkout visited by about 6% daily). Funnel conversion looks like it dropped 35% overnight, though revenue is flat. The release added logScreenView() in onResume of CheckoutActivity. Sessions from Android 13 devices show 3 events within 4 seconds. Suspicions: an analytics SDK upgrade, backend dedupe, or bots.
questions.promptHtml: Why is this happening, and how do you fix and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Debounce events for 1 second" or "blame the SDK" without explaining which lifecycle paths re-enter onResume.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is SDK auto screen tracking also on (duplicate source)? Does the event fire on rotation and after the permission/payment dialog? Is the event counted per instance or per visit? Does the dashboard definition expect "visit" or "view"? Did revenue change (is it only measurement)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Annotate the dashboard as unreliable since release; hide the funnel step from alerting; hotfix by guarding the log call.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) onResume re-fires after permission dialogs, payment sheets, share sheets, and notification-return paths; (b) rotation recreates the activity and calls onResume again; (c) SDK auto-tracking (e.g., Firebase's automatic screen_view) plus manual duplication; (d) bots (red herring since events are tied to real user sessions).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log a counter with Log.d in each callback and reproduce: open payment sheet, rotate, lock/unlock; use analytics DebugView; compare event timestamps and ga_session_id; check SDK config for auto collection.
  5. Root cause: onResume means "focused again", not "user newly arrived". It re-enters for every focus loss/gain, so the event measures focus changes, not visits.
  6. Fix: Short-term: log once per instance visit using a flag stored in the ViewModel or saved state, set after the first log, and reset in onStop only when isChangingConfigurations is false. Long-term: define a "screen view" in the analytics spec, centralize via ActivityLifecycleCallbacks or a Lifecycle observer, and disable duplicate automatic tracking.
  7. Prevention: Instrumentation test: rotate and open dialog, assert one event. Keep a spec for each event (trigger, de-dupe rule). Review checklist for analytics in onResume.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not time-based debouncing (hides bugs and drops legitimate quick revisits); not logging in onCreate alone (misses returns from background, which may count as a new visit by spec).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM wants "returned from background" counted as a new view → log on ON_START when previous ON_STOP was not due to config change.
  • Multi-window: two activities resumed → each logs; expected, define spec.
  • Same activity relaunched via singleTop → onNewIntent path needs its own rule.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A growth team spent a sprint on a "funnel regression" caused entirely by onResume logging; after the fix the metric dropped back and the real regression turned out to be 4%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests time-based debounce only.
  • Hire: Identifies onResume re-entry and rotation, guards via flag.
  • Strong hire: Adds event spec, config-change detection, SDK duplication, automated test.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Lifecycle actually dispatch to observers? What happens if I add an observer late, remove one during dispatch, or call handleLifecycleEvent from a background thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes understanding of the library you use daily, and of its main-thread and ordering invariants.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LifecycleRegistry keeps an ordered map of observers with their own state. When the owner moves to a new state, it syncs each observer forward or backward one event at a time, so each observer sees every intermediate event. An observer added late is replayed events up to the current state. It enforces main-thread access, and it tolerates adds and removes during dispatch by tracking a parent-state and a re-entrancy flag. Observers added earlier are notified first when moving up and last when moving down."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For ComponentActivity, events are dispatched by ReportFragment below API 29 and through ActivityLifecycleCallbacks (post/pre variants) on API 29+, with an extra ReportFragment safety net, so that the registry reflects the platform sequence.

Ordering guarantees:

  • Moving up (CREATED to STARTED to RESUMED): observers are called in the order added.
  • Moving down: reverse order. This mirrors stack unwinding.
  • LifecycleRegistry rejects off-main-thread calls with IllegalStateException (unless created with createUnsafe for tests).
  • Late add: with the owner at RESUMED, a new observer receives ON_CREATE, ON_START, ON_RESUME in sequence before addObserver returns, so setup code runs synchronously inside addObserver.
  • State only moves one step at a time; you cannot skip from CREATED to RESUMED.
  • Adding an observer inside a callback is handled through mAddingObserverCounter and the new observer is brought up to the current state of the dispatch, not beyond.

Practical outcome: put registrations in onCreate (before state advances) so ordering is deterministic and symmetric.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Probe : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
    override fun onCreate(o: LifecycleOwner) = Log.d("Probe", "create")
    override fun onStart(o: LifecycleOwner)  = Log.d("Probe", "start")
    override fun onResume(o: LifecycleOwner) = Log.d("Probe", "resume")
}
// In onResume():
lifecycle.addObserver(Probe())   // logs create, start, resume immediately

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing slow work in an observer's onStart that runs inside the late addObserver call.
  • Assuming only one event on late add.
  • Updating LifecycleRegistry from a worker thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why DefaultLifecycleObserver over @OnLifecycleEvent? → Annotation approach is deprecated (2.4+); reflection or codegen needed.
  2. How do you test lifecycle code? → LifecycleRegistry.createUnsafe(owner) or ActivityScenario.
  3. What if an observer throws? → Propagates into the dispatch on the main thread and crashes the app.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says observers get callbacks. Senior knows replay, ordering, thread rules and the late-add synchronous behavior.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A controller added in onResume ran its onCreate/onStart work inside addObserver, blocking the main thread unexpectedly during a transition.

questions.promptHtml: How do multi-window, Picture-in-Picture, and the multi-resume model change lifecycle assumptions, and what should apps do about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Large screens and foldables made this mainstream; many older assumptions about "one resumed activity" are false now.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Since Android 7 in split-screen, an activity that is visible but not focused is only paused, not stopped. Since Android 10 multi-resume lets every visible activity be RESUMED, and the system tells the focused one through onTopResumedActivityChanged. PiP keeps the activity paused but visible. So I put media and rendering in onStart/onStop, use onTopResumedActivityChanged for exclusive things like camera or mic priority, and handle PiP explicitly with onPictureInPictureModeChanged."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API level Behavior
24-28 Multi-window: only the focused activity resumed; the other visible one is paused
29+ Multi-resume: all visible activities resumed on devices supporting it; top-resumed one tracked by onTopResumedActivityChanged(boolean)
26+ PiP: activity paused while visible; onPictureInPictureModeChanged fires; onStop when PiP window closed

Implications:

  • Do not assume onPause means invisible.
  • Resource exclusivity: the camera/mic can be revoked from a non-focused resumed app; handle onDisconnected.
  • Video: keep playing in split-screen when visible; in PiP keep playing; stop in onStop.
  • Resizing may trigger configuration changes (smallestScreenWidthDp, screenLayout) causing recreation unless handled.
  • android:resizeableActivity default is true for targetSdk 24+; apps on foldables and tablets must tolerate arbitrary sizes. Android 16 changes orientation/resizability restrictions on large screens for apps targeting 36 (verify on developer.android.com).
  • Some OEMs opt out of multi-resume (android:resumeWhilePausing and OEM policies exist); test, don't assume.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onTopResumedActivityChanged(isTopResumed: Boolean) {   // API 29+
    super.onTopResumedActivityChanged(isTopResumed)
    if (isTopResumed) camera.requestExclusive() else camera.release()
}
override fun onPictureInPictureModeChanged(inPip: Boolean, cfg: Configuration) {
    super.onPictureInPictureModeChanged(inPip, cfg)
    controls.isVisible = !inPip
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Pausing video in onPause: in split-screen the user sees a frozen frame.
  • Calling enterPictureInPictureMode without declaring supportsPictureInPicture.
  • Assuming a single RESUMED activity in analytics.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you stop video for correct split-screen behaviour? → onStop on API 24+, with explicit PiP handling.
  2. How does the user dismissing PiP appear to the app? → onStop (or onDestroy if finishing) after leaving PiP.
  3. How do you test? → Developer options "force activities resizable", adb shell am resize-task commands, emulator foldable profiles.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows onPause/onStop. Senior brings multi-resume, top-resumed, PiP, and how camera/mic exclusivity is arbitrated.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tablet rollout showed a 3x jump in "video froze" tickets because playback paused in onPause during split-screen use.

questions.contextHtml:
Customers on a fitness app (3M MAU) report heart-rate screen "counting up by 2x, then 3x" after dismissing permission or share dialogs; battery drain is 6% per hour in the foreground. The code:

class HrActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var sm: SensorManager
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        sm = getSystemService(SensorManager::class.java)
    }
    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        sm.registerListener(
            object : SensorEventListener {
                override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { vm.onSample(e.values[0]) }
                override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
            },
            sm.getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_HEART_RATE),
            SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_NORMAL
        )
    }
    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        sm.unregisterListener(listener)   // 'listener' is a field set elsewhere, never the one registered above
    }
}

Crash rate is flat; Perfetto shows sensor batches at 3 Hz where 1 Hz is expected after two dialog cycles.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix them properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only that the listener is anonymous, or just moves the register call to onStart without fixing the ownership of the listener instance.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the duplication correlate with dialog/permission cycles (onPause/onResume without onStop)? Is the screen used in multi-window? Is there a second unregister path? What does listener refer to?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-disable the screen's sample processing duplicates by deduping on timestamps, and ship a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) mismatched pair: register in onResume, unregister in onStop; dialogs cause pause/resume without stop, so each resume registers a new anonymous listener; (b) unregister targets a different listener object, so none of the registered ones is ever removed, even on stop; (c) heart-rate sensor requires BODY_SENSORS permission, red herring; (d) SDK double-forwarding, unlikely.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add counter in onSensorChanged; adb shell dumpsys sensorservice to list active connections for the package; reproduce by opening a permission dialog 3 times.
  5. Root cause: Registration and unregistration are not symmetric: different callback pair and different instance identity. Each resume adds another listener which is never removed.
  6. Fix: One listener field, registered and unregistered in the same pair. Better, tie it to the lifecycle:
private val hrListener = object : SensorEventListener {
    override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { vm.onSample(e.values[0]) }
    override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
}
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    sm = getSystemService(SensorManager::class.java)
    lifecycle.addObserver(object : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
        override fun onStart(o: LifecycleOwner) {
            sm.registerListener(hrListener, sm.getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_HEART_RATE), SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_NORMAL)
        }
        override fun onStop(o: LifecycleOwner) { sm.unregisterListener(hrListener) }
    })
}
  1. Prevention: Lint/detekt rule for register without matching unregister; instrumented test that cycles a dialog and checks sensorservice connection count; code review rule: "pair by identity and by scope".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a Set guard to dedupe at consumer only (hides the leak and the battery drain); not registering in onCreate (runs while invisible).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not onResume/onPause pair? → Valid if sensor is only needed with focus, but then multi-window loses data; decide by product requirement.
  • Sampling should continue with screen off? → Foreground service with proper type; not an activity.
  • Using registerListener with a Handler? → Callbacks run on that thread; avoid main-thread loads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "random battery drain" bug traced to a listener list growing by one per dialog; fixing identity and pairing cut sensor wakeups by two thirds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot articulate why duplicates grow.
  • Hire: Finds asymmetric pair and instance mismatch, fixes both.
  • Strong hire: Adds lifecycle-observer ownership, dumpsys verification, and test and lint prevention.

questions.promptHtml: Does onResume mean the user can see your UI? What happens between onResume and the first drawn frame, and how do you hook the right moment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have measured startup and screen-ready time from those who only read the lifecycle diagram.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "No. onResume means the activity is resumed in ATMS. The window is added and made visible just after onResume, and the first measure/layout/draw happens on the next Choreographer frame. So views have no size in the first onResume, and the screen may still be blank. For 'screen is visible' I use a pre-draw or first-draw listener, for 'user can interact' I use onWindowFocusChanged or reportFullyDrawn, and for measurement I use ViewTreeObserver or doOnLayout."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sequence for a freshly created activity:

onCreate -> onStart -> onResume
   -> WindowManager.addView / ViewRootImpl.setView  (in handleResumeActivity, after onResume)
   -> first Choreographer frame: performTraversals (measure, layout, draw)
   -> onAttachedToWindow, onWindowFocusChanged(true) arrive around here
   -> frame presented by SurfaceFlinger on a later vsync

Consequences:

  • view.width is 0 in onCreate/onStart/onResume on first run.
  • Work placed in onResume delays the first frame because the main thread must finish it before performTraversals runs. Startup latency (covered by the profiling chunks) is bounded by it.
  • To act after first draw, use view.doOnPreDraw {} (androidx.core), ViewTreeObserver.addOnPreDrawListener, or Window.OnFrameMetricsAvailableListener for measurement. Activity.reportFullyDrawn() (API 19+) tells the system the app is fully usable, for startup metrics.
  • Splash screen API (Android 12+) holds the splash until the first frame is drawn, or until setKeepOnScreenCondition returns false.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onResume() {
    super.onResume()
    binding.root.doOnPreDraw {          // androidx.core.view
        // first frame about to be drawn: sizes are valid, UI is about to appear
        metrics.markScreenReady()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Measuring "screen load time" at onResume and reporting artificially good numbers.
  • Reading view sizes in onResume on first launch.
  • Putting disk reads in onResume, which delays the first frame.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do I get true time-to-first-frame? → reportFullyDrawn and frame metrics, plus system startup metrics (see the profiling chunk).
  2. What is onPostResume for? → Called after the fragment manager has resumed child fragments; rarely needed.
  3. Does onWindowFocusChanged always come after onResume? → For a new window typically yes; not guaranteed in all multi-window cases.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says visible at onResume. Senior gives the window-add timing, first-traversal behavior, and the correct hooks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "time to screen" KPI improved 300 ms overnight after a refactor, only because the timer stopped at onResume rather than first draw.

questions.contextHtml: A video app (5M MAU) pauses playback in onPause and releases the player in onStop, written for API 23. Tablets and foldables are now 22% of sessions; 31% of those use split-screen. Tickets: "video freezes when I type in the other app", plus a 1-star review wave. Another report: in Picture-in-Picture, video disappears after tapping the PiP "close" button but audio continues for about 3 seconds. A proposal on the table: move everything to onResume/onPause "because Google says so".
questions.promptHtml: Decide where playback should start, pause and release, and justify it, including PiP.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks one callback pair dogmatically, doesn't separate pause from release, ignores PiP and API levels.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is minSdk (is API 23 still supported)? Do we support PiP and background audio? Is the player owned by the Activity or a service (Media3 MediaSession)? Is DRM or hardware decoder count a constraint?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop pausing on onPause when the activity is in multi-window or PiP (isInMultiWindowMode, isInPictureInPictureMode); ship quickly behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) onPause is firing on mere focus loss in split-screen; (b) PiP close leaves player alive until the activity is destroyed; (c) release in onStop but PiP close does not always stop the activity immediately; (d) decoder starvation (red herring unless multiple players).
  4. How I'd verify each: Use logs of lifecycle + onPictureInPictureModeChanged, adb am commands to enter split-screen, tablet emulator, dumpsys activity activities to see state per task.
  5. Root cause: The old rule "pause in onPause" assumed onPause means invisible; on API 24+ it only means focus lost.
  6. Fix: On API 24+: initialize/prepare in onStart, release in onStop; do not pause in onPause when in multi-window or PiP; pause in onStop (or release) otherwise. Below API 24, use onResume/onPause (Media3 guidance). For PiP: handle onPictureInPictureModeChanged, and on dismissal (activity stopped with lifecycle.currentState == CREATED after PiP) release immediately.
override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT > 23) initPlayer() }
override fun onResume() { super.onResume(); if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT <= 23 || player == null) initPlayer() }
override fun onPause() { super.onPause(); if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT <= 23) releasePlayer() }
override fun onStop() { super.onStop(); if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT > 23) releasePlayer() }
  1. Prevention: Device lab matrix including foldable and split-screen; instrumentation tests with ActivityScenario and window resize commands; playback state analytics segmented by windowing mode.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "play while screen is off" via activity (belongs in a foreground media service with MediaSession); not keep the player forever in a singleton (leaks, DRM licenses, decoder limits).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Background audio requested → move the player to a MediaSessionService with a foreground service of type mediaPlayback.
  • Two video activities in multi-resume → each needs its own decoder; limit concurrent players.
  • Gesture to pause when another window gains focus → use onTopResumedActivityChanged.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rewrite to Media3 deleted three bespoke pause hacks and moved the player into a service; split-screen complaints vanished within one release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Always onResume/onPause".
  • Hire: Chooses onStart/onStop on API 24+, mentions PiP.
  • Strong hire: Adds multi-resume, service ownership, API-level split and testing plan.

questions.contextHtml: A banking app (1.2M DAU) shows a PIN prompt when returning from background after 30 s. After a release, users reported being asked for the PIN on every screen rotation, and security logged 4x more "session expired" events. The implementation counts onActivityStarted/onActivityStopped via ActivityLifecycleCallbacks and starts a 30 s Handler.postDelayed timer when the count hits zero. The timer works in testing (screen off, wait 30 s). Rotation reproduces on 100% of Android 13 devices. A second report: on phones left idle for 10 minutes the PIN sometimes did not appear at all.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident analysis: causes, fix, and how to prevent recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "add a delay" for rotation and "use a wake lock" for the missing prompt.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it per-process or are there multiple processes? Does the PIN gate rely on a timer or on timestamps? What is the security requirement exactly (lock after 30 s of not being visible)? Does the lock trigger on any activity stop, including the permission dialog flow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix to ignore stop events when isChangingConfigurations is true and stop using timers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) rotation causes stop of old instance before start of new one, count hits zero and timer fires logic or immediate lock; (b) timer lives on the main Looper: when the app is backgrounded and the process is frozen/killed or the device sleeps, postDelayed uses uptime that stops in deep sleep, so the timer is late or never; (c) system dialog flows bounce the count; (d) clock changes (red herring if using elapsedRealtime).
  4. How I'd verify each: Logs of each callback with isChangingConfigurations; reproduce with rotation, with screen-off for 10 minutes, with adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle; check the Handler delay uses uptimeMillis (stops during sleep).
  5. Root cause: Using activity counting without debounce, and using an uptime-based timer for a wall-clock policy.
  6. Fix: Use ProcessLifecycleOwner for foreground state (700 ms debounce for config changes). On ON_STOP save SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() (includes deep sleep). On ON_START compute the delta; if over 30 s, show the PIN. Persist the timestamp so process death also forces re-lock (treat a null timestamp as locked).
override fun onStop(owner: LifecycleOwner) { prefs.lastBackground = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() }
override fun onStart(owner: LifecycleOwner) {
    val t = prefs.lastBackground
    if (t == null || SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - t > 30_000) showPin()
}

Note elapsedRealtime resets at reboot; handle with a boot-count or treat newer-than-now as locked. 7. Prevention: Test matrix: rotation, split-screen, share sheet, process death; fail-closed policy (unknown means locked); a unit test of the session policy with a fake clock. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a background service just to run a timer; not System.currentTimeMillis (user can change the clock); not a longer delay hack for rotation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Biometric prompt itself pauses the activity → exclude biometric/system dialog flows, use state flag during prompt.
  • Multi-process app → state per process; centralize the policy.
  • Compliance wants lock when app goes to the recents screen → treat onPause + window focus loss separately and apply FLAG_SECURE for the screenshot problem.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The root fix was to model the lock as a timestamp comparison with fail-closed defaults, which also covered cases never tested like OEM task killers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds longer delay.
  • Hire: Fixes rotation via ProcessLifecycleOwner and timestamps.
  • Strong hire: Handles reboot/clock/process death, fail-closed design, test plan and recents screen.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace app loads the home feed from onResume (vm.refresh()). DAU is 5M, average 14 resumes per session. A push campaign targeted at 3M users led to API p95 latency rising from 180 ms to 2.4 s and 429s from the gateway, though request volume per user looked normal in earlier release tests. Crashlytics shows nothing. Backend logs show bursts of 3-4 identical requests per user within 2 seconds. Android Vitals shows normal ANR rates. A teammate suggests caching on the server.
questions.promptHtml: What is generating the load, and how do you fix it at the client?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Server-side caching only, or adding a client-side if (time < 1s) return debounce.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What triggers the refresh path (onResume only or also onStart)? Is refresh conditioned on staleness? Are there rotation or dialog flows? Is the campaign deep-linking into the home activity (singleTop and onNewIntent)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side rate limit on feed endpoint per user plus a remote config to disable resume refresh.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) every focus regain (permission prompt, notification shade does not count, share sheet, deep link return) triggers a refresh; (b) rotation recreates, ViewModel refreshes again; (c) push-open path starts the activity, triggers onCreate init and onResume refresh both; (d) retry storms from the 429s themselves (feedback loop).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log per-callback with request IDs; Charles/mitmproxy on a device cycling dialogs; server logs grouped by device ID and timestamp; check retry/backoff logic.
  5. Root cause: Using a focus callback as a "data is stale" signal. 14 resumes per session times 5M DAU yields 70M resume-triggered refreshes per day, versus perhaps 15M if tied to real staleness: roughly 5x amplification, worse during the campaign when sessions are short and frequent.
  6. Fix: Short-term: refresh only if now - lastSuccessfulLoad > TTL (e.g., 60 s) using elapsedRealtime in the ViewModel/repository. Long-term: load on first subscription (WhileSubscribed), explicit pull-to-refresh, push or realtime invalidation for freshness, request coalescing in the repository, exponential backoff with jitter on 429/5xx.
  7. Prevention: Load test in the client: count requests per scripted user journey (rotate, dialog, background/return) and assert a budget in CI; dashboards for requests-per-session; a lint/review rule "no network in onResume".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a naive time debounce (loses meaningful refresh after long background); not disabling refresh entirely (stale feed is a product regression).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product requires "fresh after 5 min away" → TTL anchored on onStop timestamp; refresh on ON_START only past TTL.
  • Realtime feed via socket → connect in onStart/onStop; the repository exposes a Flow.
  • Same bug in Fragments (ViewPager) → use viewLifecycleOwner and setMaxLifecycle, not onResume per page.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single "refresh on resume" line was responsible for roughly 60% of the feed endpoint traffic; replacing it with staleness-based loading cut backend cost and removed the incident class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Server cache only.
  • Hire: Identifies resume amplification, adds TTL.
  • Strong hire: Does the math, backoff/coalescing, structural fix (state in ViewModel/repository) and request-budget tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A team migrates 40 screens from startActivityForResult/onActivityResult to the Activity Result API in a staged rollout (10% then 50%). At 10%, a new crash appears at 0.4% of sessions on the migrated screens:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: LifecycleOwner com.shop.CartActivity@3f2a1 is attempting to register while current state is RESUMED. LifecycleOwners must call register before they are STARTED.
    at androidx.activity.result.ActivityResultRegistry.register(ActivityResultRegistry.java:...)
    at androidx.activity.ComponentActivity.registerForActivityResult(...)
    at com.shop.CartActivity.onPromoClicked(CartActivity.kt:88)

Also QA reports that after "Don't keep activities" or real process death, the chosen photo is sometimes delivered to the wrong screen's handler on the profile screen, which registers launchers conditionally.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both failures and describe the safe migration pattern and rollout.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps the register call in try/catch, or registers in onStart.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where exactly is register called (click handler, lazy getter, if block)? Are fragments involved? Are contracts custom? Do any screens register different numbers of launchers by feature flag?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the rollout at 10%, hotfix the offending screens by hoisting the registration into property initializers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) registration inside event handlers or lazy blocks executed after STARTED, which throws; (b) conditional registration changes key order, and the registry restores callbacks by key after recreation, so a result is delivered to the wrong callback; (c) callbacks capturing the activity instance (leak, stale closure); (d) a library double-registering (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Stack trace line numbers; a test enabling "Don't keep activities" and adb shell am kill between launching and returning; review for conditionals before register calls; LeakCanary for captured callbacks.
  5. Root cause: Launchers are registered through the registry using auto-generated keys derived from registration order, which must be stable and happen before STARTED. Registering late violates the lifecycle rule; conditional registration changes the key sequence, so restored pending results are mapped to different callbacks.
  6. Fix: Register unconditionally, in the property initializer or onCreate, one launcher per contract; make the callback consult state (ViewModel) to decide behavior. For dynamic cases, use register(key, owner, contract, callback) on activityResultRegistry with a fixed string key.
class CartActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val promo = registerForActivityResult(PromoContract()) { vm.onPromo(it) }   // unconditional, early
    private fun onPromoClicked() = promo.launch(Unit)                                    // launch anywhere
}
  1. Prevention: Lint check (androidx activity lint flags registerForActivityResult inside non-lifecycle-safe locations); a migration test per screen that kills the process mid-flow; keep rollout staged with crash-free thresholds.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang migration; not keeping both mechanisms on the same screen (request code collisions); not a singleton for launchers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need a result in a ViewModel or non-UI class → pass the launcher or an abstraction (contract wrapper), do not register from non-owners.
  • Result arrives while stopped → delivered when STARTED; make the handler idempotent.
  • Fragment shares an activity's launcher → each fragment registers its own; fragment keys include its unique identifier but conditional order issues remain.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The staged rollout caught a 0.4% crash before 50%; the key-order bug would have been silent data misrouting, which is why process-death tests were added to the migration checklist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: try/catch or register in onStart.
  • Hire: Hoists registration early and unconditionally.
  • Strong hire: Explains key stability, process-death delivery, lint, staged rollout and idempotent callbacks.
